title: Om: three sounds and a silence
hook: Death gives a boy one word, and two schools hear its silence differently
carry: om holds waking, dream, sleep, and the silent self
tomorrow: why does an Upanishad stop to talk about honey?

segments.voice: Yesterday, ayam atma brahma came through the back door: neti neti, not this, not this. Today the Mandukya gives the same self a sound, and then takes the sound away.

A boy waits three nights at Death's door, and Death, who kept a guest waiting, owes him three wishes. In the Katha Upanishad, Nachiketa spends the last one asking what happens to a person after death. Somewhere in his answer, Yama, the lord of death, gives him one word: the word all the Vedas point to, he says, is Om. The Mandukya Upanishad takes that syllable apart: ah, oo, mmm, then a beat of silence. It calls the silence the fourth part, the heart of it all. Two great schools of Vedanta agree on that much. They don't agree on what lives in the silence.
screen: `THREE NIGHTS AT DEATH'S DOOR.` → `THE WORD ALL THE VEDAS POINT TO: OM.` → `TWO SCHOOLS, ONE SILENCE.`

segments.voice: First, the text. The Mandukya lays this self over Om. A is waking, the self that deals with the world outside. U is dreaming, at home in an inner world. M is deep sleep, where everything gathers into one. And the fourth has no sound part at all. It is peaceful, kind, not two. That, the text says, is the self. Now the two readings. Advaita teachers read the Mandukya through verses tradition credits to Gaudapada, and through Shankara. For them, the fourth is the one self that was there all along. Waking, dream and sleep pass across it like weather across the sky, and not two means just that: there is no second thing. Madhva's school reads the same Upanishad and hears the Lord in it. The quarters, it says, name forms of Vishnu, who is present in waking, dream and sleep and stands beyond them all. The self who knows him is real, depends on him, and never becomes him. Both schools take the Mandukya as scripture. Both chant the same Om. One hears the silence as the self with nothing beside it; the other hears the Lord holding everything that is. And this is why Hindus begin and end prayer, study, even a wedding card, with Om: in this teaching, one syllable holds every state you'll ever be in, and the quiet beneath them all.
screen: `A, U, M: WAKING, DREAM, SLEEP.` · `THE FOURTH: PEACEFUL, NOT TWO.` · `ADVAITA: ONE SELF, NO SECOND.` · `MADHVA: THE LORD, BEYOND ALL THREE.`

segments.voice: If you're somewhere you can, say Om once, slowly, out loud: ah, oo, mmm. Then stay in the silence after it for a few breaths before the next one. Keep going at your own pace, listening as closely to the quiet as to the sound.
Ayam atma brahma, through the Mandukya: Om's three sounds as waking, dream and sleep, and a fourth that makes no sound, peaceful, kind, not two.
Something to keep: Om holds waking, dream and sleep, and the silence after it is the self. Two schools hear that silence in their own ways. Until tomorrow.

Mandukya.meaning: a short Upanishad that lays the self over the sound Om

Gaudapada.meaning: a teacher tradition credits with verses on the Mandukya

Madhva.meaning: founder of a Vedanta school that keeps God and self distinct

Vishnu.meaning: the god Madhva's school worships as the Lord

Nachiketa.meaning: the boy who questions Death in the Katha Upanishad

sources.ref: Katha Upanishad 1.1.20 (Nachiketa's third wish: what becomes of a person after death); 1.2.15 (the word all the Vedas declare is Om)

Mandukya Upanishad 7–12 (the fourth: peaceful, kind, not two; A, U and M as waking, dream and deep sleep; the fourth without a sound part)
